input: Obtaining a sample that represents a powder blend is more subtle than it first appears, because a blend is not uniform from place to place, and any approach that ignores this risks misleading results. Whenever a blend is moved, tipped or allowed to stand, the coarse and fine particles tend to separate: the fines sift downwards through the voids between the larger particles, while the coarse particles roll towards the outside of a heap or the wall of a container. As a result, material at the surface differs from material at depth, and material at the centre differs from material at the edge, even where the blend was uniform when made. Samples are therefore taken from points spread throughout the mass, at depth as well as at the surface. Where the equipment permits, increments may be taken from the moving stream during transfer or discharge, since a stream in motion presents every part of the batch in turn, ensuring that no region is left untested because of its position. Each taking, referred to as an increment, is small beside the batch, and a sample is formed by combining many increments and mixing them thoroughly before any portion is withdrawn for testing. A single grab sample, one scoop taken from one location, is particularly misleading, because it reports only the segregated state of the spot it was taken from; a result obtained this way can clear a batch that is off composition elsewhere, or condemn one that is actually sound. It should be noted that no numerical limits are stated here, since the limits governing a product are held in the site's permit and are applied at that level rather than in a general passage of this kind.
